newsitem.title: GREECE: Papandreou family feud mars memorial.
newsitem.headline: Papandreou family feud mars memorial.

text.p: Memorial events planned by Greece's ruling socialists to mark a year since the death of their founder Andreas Papandreou have been marred by squabbles between his children and his widow over his legacy.

The row between the constantly black-clad, former Olympic Airways flight attendant Dimitra Liani and Papandreou's four children has dominated the news and overshadowed retrospectives about the life of one of Greece's great political leaders.
Crowded in a small chapel at Athens's First Cemetery for a memorial service on Sunday, the feuding sides of the late leader's family hardly exchanged a glance.
"This is a day when we must honour and respect Andreas Papandreou, honour his great work for Greece and remember what he gave to us," Prime Minister Costas Simitis told reporters at the cemetery.
His words apparently answered several statements issued by Liani, criticising party-planned commemorative events for excluding her and not being open enough to the public.
Liani, who was catapulted from obscurity to Greece's first lady and Papandreou's chief of staff, attended ceremonies on the island of Crete, where they used to spend holidays together.
She did not attend an event on Papandreou's political life in Athens, where the children and their mother, Margaret, held centre stage, or ceremonies in his home town of Patras.

Socialist party members, who adore Papandreou with near-religious fervour, have expressed dismay over the way the family feud has been marring his image but others say the row matches his adventurous personal life.
"He was not exactly a model of morality. What we see happening with his family is a direct result of the way he lived his life," political analyst Thanos Veremis told Reuters.

Liani was about half Papandreou's age when they met as she was serving him drinks on an airliner in 1988. He married her in 1989 after a public extra-marital affair that partly cost him an election defeat after eight years in power.

The children had been discreet about Liani while their father was alive but openly expressed their distaste after his death in June 1996. Papandreou's son Nikos described her in comments to a Western newspaper as a "power-hungry vulture".
Only Papandreou's older son George, a deputy foreign minister, has tried to keep out of the public row.
Liani has worked to secure her place on the board of a planned Papandreou Foundation, an idea that makes his children cringe, with statements to the press and public appearences.

They have resorted to legal moves to reverse the sale of their grandmother's house, which Papandreou sold to build Liani a controversial pink villa, after finding a lost will that leaves the property to them.

The children say they want to give the house, where Papandreou was arrested before their eyes at the start of a seven-year dictatorship in 1967, to the foundation devoted to their father's memory. The case will be tried this fall.

Liani's meteoric rise, unpolished ways and published nude sunbathing pictures never gained her much public sympathy but her efforts to stay in the limelight with public displays of grief have angered even her defenders.
